facts.statement: Nothronychus lived during the Turonian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Cretaceous (Turonian)

facts.statement: The type species Nothronychus mckinleyi was described by James Kirkland and Douglas G. Wolfe in 2001.
facts.quote: The type species, Nothronychus mckinleyi, was described by James Kirkland and Douglas G. Wolfe in 2001.

facts.statement: Nothronychus fossils were found near the New Mexico-Arizona border in the Zuni Basin within the Moreno Hill Formation.
facts.quote: It was recovered near New Mexico's border with Arizona, in an area known as the Zuni Basin, from rocks assigned to the Moreno Hill Formation, dating to the Turonian stage of the Late Cretaceous.

facts.statement: Nothronychus is a genus of therizinosaurid theropod dinosaurs named for its "slothful claw".
facts.quote: Nothronychus (meaning "slothful claw") is a genus of therizinosaurid theropod dinosaurs

facts.statement: Nothronychus was a bulky herbivore with wide hips, four forward-facing toes, an elongated neck, and prominent arms with sharp claws.
facts.quote: Like other therizinosaurids, Nothronychus was likely a bulky herbivore with wide, sloth-like hips (resembling those of the unrelated ornithischians), feet with four forward-facing toes, elongated necks, and prominent arms with sharp claws.

facts.statement: The first fossils attributed to Nothronychus were discovered at the Haystack Butte site in the Zuni Basin, New Mexico.
facts.quote: The first fossil evidence later attributed to Nothronychus was discovered by a team of paleontologists working in the Zuni Basin of New Mexico at the Haystack Butte site, Moreno Hill Formation.

facts.statement: The name Nothronychus combines Greek words meaning "slothful" and "claw".
facts.quote: The generic name, Nothronychus, is derived from Greek νωθρός (, meaning slothful) and ὄνυξ (onyx, meaning claw).

facts.statement: The species name mckinleyi honors rancher Bobby McKinley, whose land yielded the fossils.
facts.quote: The specific name, mckinleyi, honours rancher Bobby McKinley on whose land the fossil findings were made.

facts.statement: A more complete specimen was discovered in 2000 in southern Utah by resident Merle Graffam.
facts.quote: A second, more complete specimen, UMNH VP 16420, was discovered from the Tropic Shale Formation (dating to the early Turonian stage) of southern Utah in 2000 by Merle Graffam, a resident of Big Water, Utah.

facts.statement: Nothronychus graffami was formally named by Lindsay Zanno and colleagues in 2009.
facts.quote: The specimen was classified and named as the new species Nothronychus graffami by Lindsay Zanno and colleagues in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society B on 15 July 2009.

facts.statement: Nothronychus was the first therizinosaur discovered in the Americas, as all previous finds came from China and Mongolia.
facts.quote: All previous therizinosaur fossils had come from China and Mongolia.

facts.statement: Nothronychus was a medium-sized dinosaur measuring 4.2 to 5.3 meters long and weighing 800 to 1200 kilograms.
facts.quote: Nothronychus is a medium-sized therizinosaur, measuring 4.2 - 5.3 m long and weighing 800 - 1200 kg.

facts.statement: Nothronychus had large arms with dexterous hands bearing curved, sharp claws up to 30 cm long.
facts.quote: Its arms were relatively large with dexterous hands equipped with up to 30 cm long curved and sharply-pointed claws on their fingers.

facts.statement: Nothronychus belongs to the theropod group Coelurosauria, which is mainly composed of carnivorous dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Nothronychus were members of the Coelurosauria, the theropod group composed mainly by carnivorous dinosaurs.

facts.statement: Nothronychus is part of the Maniraptora subgroup, a group of theropods that evolved into plant-eaters.
facts.quote: Nothronychus form part of the sub-group Maniraptora, theropods which evolved into partial omnivores and, in the case of Nothronychus and their family, plant-eaters.

facts.statement: Nothronychus mckinleyi was assigned to the family Therizinosauridae in 2001 based on derived features.
facts.quote: Nothronychus mckinleyi was in 2001 assigned to the Therizinosauridae given the derived features of the genus.

facts.statement: Cladistic analysis recovered both species of Nothronychus as a sister group.
facts.quote: The cladistic analysis performed recovered both N. mckinleyi and N. graffami as a sister group.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Nothronychus was herbivorous, citing features like a keratinous beak, small skulls, and a large gut capacity.
facts.quote: In 2009, Zanno and colleagues stated therizinosaurs were the most-widely regarded candidates for herbivory among theropods based on the small, densely packed, coarse serrations; lance-shaped teeth with a relatively low replacement rate; a well-developed keratinous beak; long neck for browsing; relatively small skulls; a very large gut capacity as indicated by the rib circumference at the trunk and the outwards flaring processes of the ilia; and the notable lack of cursorial adaptations in the hind limbs.

facts.statement: Studies indicate Nothronychus hands were effective for piercing or pulling down vegetation to access food.
facts.quote: In 2014, Lautenschlager tested the biomechanical function of multiple therizinosaur claws. He noted that the hands of some therizinosaurids (such as Nothronyhus or Therizinosaurus) were more effective when piercing or pulling down vegetation.

facts.statement: A 2024 study claims Nothronychus is herbivorous based on a retroverted pubis, suggesting this trait evolved multiple times in maniraptorans.
facts.quote: In 2024, Smith and Gillette claimed that Nothronychus is herbivorous on the basis of retroverted pubis, analogous with the postacetabular bar of ornithischians, and that many characters of Nothronychus including the pubic condition are absent in earlier therizinosaurs like Falcarius, so such structures would have evolved multiple times throughout the maniraptoran lineage.

facts.statement: Research from 2015 identified three functional muscle groups at the neck base of Nothronychus: dorsiflexors, lateroflexors, and ventroflexors.
facts.quote: In 2015, Smith studied the myology and functional morphology of the craniocervical junction of N. mckinleyi. The craniocervical muscles can be subdivided into functional groups as dorsiflexors, lateroflexors, and ventroflexors.

facts.statement: Nothronychus had a long, S-shaped neck with small neural spines, similar to ostriches and Diplodocus.
facts.quote: With small neural spines relative to the long S-shaped neck, its neck pattern was similar to that of ostriches and Diplodocus.

facts.statement: Nothronychus possessed an incipiently opisthopubic pelvis, which researchers associate with extensive modifications to its muscular system.
facts.quote: In the same year, Smith reconstructed the hindlimb musculature of N. graffami. Nothronychus had a pelvis that is incipiently opisthopubic, which Smith expects to be associated with the muscular system's extensive modification.

facts.statement: A 2023 study suggests Nothronychus walked with most motion occurring at the knee and limited movement at the femur.
facts.quote: A 2023 study by Smith and Gillette suggests that much of the walking motion for N. graffami took place at the knee when moving, with movement at the femur limited.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Nothronychus had a waddling gait and a digitigrade stance, though plantigrade walking remains a possibility.
facts.quote: This same study also suggests a waddling gait for Nothronychus, and a digitigrade stance, though plantigrade walking could not entirely be ruled out.

facts.statement: Studies of brain endocasts indicate Nothronychus had well-developed senses of smell, hearing, and balance useful for foraging.
facts.quote: In 2012, paleontologist Stephan Lautenschlager and team examined the endocasts (brain cavity) of several therizinosaurs (including N. mckinleyi), concluding that most members had well developed senses of smell, hearing, and balance, mostly useful for foraging.

facts.statement: Analysis of the braincase suggests Nothronychus had large pneumatic chambers optimized for receiving low-frequency sounds, possibly infrasound.
facts.quote: In 2018, the holotype braincase of Nothronychus mckinleyi was re-examined by Smith and colleagues updating numerous basicranial and soft-tissues aspects. They noted that the braincase has particularly large pneumatic chambers on the sensorial areas, suggesting that the increased tympanic systems would result in optimal low frequency sound reception, possibly infrasound, and in complex social behavior.

facts.statement: While hearing estimates may be exaggerated, Nothronychus retained elongated semicircular canals associated with an active, predatory lifestyle.
facts.quote: They stated, however, that these estimates could be slightly exaggerated. Also, N. mckinleyi retained elongated semicircular canals in the ear, which are more related to an active, predatory life-style.

facts.statement: Based on comparisons with Erlikosaurus, Nothronychus likely had a horizontal head posture enabling binocular vision.
facts.quote: Finally, based on Erlikosaurus, N. mckinleyi may have had a relatively horizontal head posture, which is associated with overlapping visual fields and binocular vision, given the orientation of the horizontal semicircular canal relative to the horizontal orientation of the occipital condyle.

facts.statement: Researchers believe the air sacs in Nothronychus supported an avian-style respiratory system rather than weight reduction or thermoregulation.
facts.quote: The researchers considered that the pneumatization in therizinosaurs wouldn't have been related to weight reduction or thermoregulation, but to an avian-style respiratory system.

facts.statement: Nothronychus fossils are found in the Moreno Hill Formation, an environment characterized by tectonic upheaval, volcanic activity, and a humid climate.
facts.quote: Specimens of Nothronychus are known from the Moreno Hill Formation which documents a time of tectonic upheaval, volcanic activities, humid paleoclimate, and North American coastal margin shifts.

facts.statement: Nothronychus lived alongside dinosaurs such as Suskityrannus, Zuniceratops, Jeyawati, and ankylosaurs in the Moreno Hill Formation.
facts.quote: Other dinosaurs fossils recovered from this formation are Suskityrannus, Zuniceratops, Jeyawati, and undescribed ankylosaur remains.
